findings.claim: Its working definition ... names decision-making under uncertainty as the problem space
findings.failure_mode: loosened attribution: the definition names complex problems, not decision-making
findings.evidence: Deep ref L25: 'Scrum is a lightweight framework that helps people, teams and organizations generate value through adaptive solutions for complex problems'. The definition names complex problems and value generation; decision-making appears only in the empiricism gloss (L31).
findings.fix: correct: Its working definition ... names complex problems as the problem space, and its foundation in empiricism ... makes the framework a structured discipline for making decisions when prediction is unreliable.

findings.claim: low-transparency artefacts produce decisions that "diminish value and increase risk" [V]
findings.failure_mode: hardened claim around a verbatim fragment
findings.evidence: Deep ref L37: 'Artifacts that have low transparency can lead to decisions that diminish value and increase risk'. 'can lead to' becomes 'produce'.
findings.fix: correct: low-transparency artefacts "can lead to decisions that diminish value and increase risk" [V]

findings.claim: The Product Owner, and only the Product Owner, orders the Product Backlog, defines the Product Goal, and may cancel the Sprint.
findings.failure_mode: omits the delegation clause; conflates doing the work with holding the accountability
findings.evidence: Deep ref L74-76: the PO is accountable for developing the Product Goal and ordering items, but 'may do the above work or may delegate the responsibility to others. Regardless, the Product Owner remains accountable'. Only cancellation is reserved exclusively ('Only the Product Owner has the authority to cancel the Sprint', L115).
findings.fix: correct: The Product Owner alone is accountable for ordering the Product Backlog and for the Product Goal (the work may be delegated; the accountability may not), and only the Product Owner may cancel the Sprint.

findings.claim: The Scrum Master decides nothing about the product but is accountable for the team's ability to make decisions empirically.
findings.failure_mode: accountability paraphrased into a different accountability
findings.evidence: Deep ref L84-86: the Scrum Master is accountable 'for establishing Scrum as defined in the Scrum Guide' and 'for the Scrum Team's effectiveness'. The Guide states no 'decides nothing about the product' rule and names no accountability for 'the team's ability to make decisions empirically'.
findings.fix: correct: The Scrum Master holds no product accountability; they are accountable for establishing Scrum and for the Scrum Team's effectiveness, which includes 'Helping establish empirical product planning for a complex environment' [V].

findings.claim: "The Product Owner is one person, not a committee" [V] is the most direct expression of the principle that a complex decision needs a single accountable owner
findings.failure_mode: distillation's principle presented as the Guide's
findings.evidence: Deep ref L80: the Guide states the constraint and that stakeholders change the Backlog by 'trying to convince the Product Owner'; it states no general principle about complex decisions needing a single owner.
findings.fix: correct: "The Product Owner is one person, not a committee" [V]: the Guide gives one accountable owner for the Product Backlog, even when many stakeholders want to influence it.

findings.claim: the Daily Scrum's structure is "at the sole discretion of the Developers" [V]
findings.failure_mode: verbatim quote attached to the wrong concept
findings.evidence: Deep ref L129: 'at the sole discretion of the Developers' is Sprint Planning Topic Three (how selected items become an Increment). The Daily Scrum wording is L141: 'The Developers can select whatever structure and techniques they want'.
findings.fix: correct: the Daily Scrum's structure is theirs to choose ("The Developers can select whatever structure and techniques they want" [V])

findings.claim: A decision made on a low-transparency artefact will "diminish value and increase risk." [V]
findings.failure_mode: hardened claim around a verbatim fragment
findings.evidence: Deep ref L37: 'can lead to decisions that diminish value and increase risk'.
findings.fix: correct: A decision made on a low-transparency artefact "can lead to decisions that diminish value and increase risk" [V].

findings.claim: The single-owner constraint exists because complex decisions need a single accountable owner, even when many stakeholders want input.
findings.failure_mode: rationale attributed to the framework that the source does not give
findings.evidence: Deep ref L80 states the constraint with no rationale. Nothing in the deep ref or source says why the PO is one person.
findings.fix: strip

findings.claim: Sprint Planning as three sequential decisions ... The order matters: value before scope before plan.
findings.failure_mode: sequencing rule added to the source
findings.evidence: Deep ref L123-L131: Sprint Planning 'addresses the following topics' One, Two, Three; the Guide does not say they run in sequence or that order matters, and requires only that the Sprint Goal be 'finalized prior to the end of Sprint Planning' (L125).
findings.fix: correct: Sprint Planning as three Topics ... The Guide numbers them why, what, how; the Sprint Goal must be finalised before Sprint Planning ends.

findings.claim: The Guide treats these as conditions for empiricism: openness about challenges enables transparency; courage to do the right thing enables adaptation; respect for capable, independent colleagues enables the self-management that adaptation requires.
findings.failure_mode: one-to-one value-to-pillar mapping attributed to the Guide
findings.evidence: Deep ref L17, L50-52: the Guide says that when the values are embodied 'the empirical Scrum pillars of transparency, inspection, and adaptation come to life building trust'. It does not pair particular values with particular pillars.
findings.fix: correct: The Guide treats these as conditions for empiricism: when they are embodied, "the empirical Scrum pillars of transparency, inspection, and adaptation come to life building trust" [V]. (Pairing openness with transparency or courage with adaptation is this distillation's reading.)

findings.claim: Low transparency yields decisions that "diminish value and increase risk." [V]
findings.failure_mode: hardened claim around a verbatim fragment
findings.evidence: Deep ref L37: 'can lead to decisions that diminish value and increase risk'.
findings.fix: correct: Low transparency "can lead to decisions that diminish value and increase risk" [V].

findings.claim: Sprint Planning (8 hours), Sprint Review (4 hours), Sprint Retrospective (3 hours)
findings.failure_mode: figures stripped of their qualifier
findings.evidence: Deep ref L133, L153, L163, L228-230: each is a 'maximum ... for a one-month Sprint. For shorter Sprints, the event is usually shorter'.
findings.fix: correct: Sprint Planning (max 8 hours), Sprint Review (max 4 hours), Sprint Retrospective (max 3 hours), each for a one-month Sprint and usually shorter for shorter Sprints

findings.claim: Consider Sprint cancellation only if Sprint Goal obsolete
findings.failure_mode: sufficient condition hardened into necessary condition
findings.evidence: Deep ref L115: 'A Sprint could be cancelled if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete'. The Guide names this ground; it does not say 'only if'.
findings.fix: correct: Consider Sprint cancellation when the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete

findings.claim: it is "not a status update."
findings.failure_mode: phrase in quotation marks that is not in the source
findings.evidence: 'status update' does not occur in the converted source or the deep ref. The Guide's wording (deep L151) is 'the Scrum Team should avoid limiting it to a presentation'.
findings.fix: correct: the Scrum Team "should avoid limiting it to a presentation" [V].

findings.claim: Follow-up: write an explicit DoD; apply it mechanically at the Sprint boundary.
findings.failure_mode: applied guidance resting on a premise the Guide contradicts in part
findings.evidence: Deep ref L206, L212: 'The moment a Product Backlog item meets the Definition of Done, an Increment is born'; 'an Increment may be delivered to stakeholders prior to the end of the Sprint'. The DoD applies per item, not at the Sprint boundary.
findings.fix: correct: Follow-up: write an explicit DoD; apply it to every item before it counts as Done.

findings.claim: A Sprint cancellation question: only the Product Owner can; only if the Sprint Goal is obsolete.
findings.failure_mode: sufficient condition hardened into necessary condition
findings.evidence: Deep ref L115: 'A Sprint could be cancelled if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete. Only the Product Owner has the authority to cancel the Sprint'. The first half is exact; 'only if' is not in the Guide.
findings.fix: correct: only the Product Owner can, and the Guide's named ground is an obsolete Sprint Goal.

findings.claim: The engineering manager's mid-Sprint reordering [of the Sprint Backlog] is a Product Owner responsibility violation ... they do not directly edit the backlog or Sprint scope.
findings.failure_mode: Sprint Backlog and Product Backlog accountabilities conflated
findings.evidence: Scenario (L137) has the manager reordering the Sprint Backlog. Deep ref L196: 'The Sprint Backlog is a plan by and for the Developers'; L200: scope changes are negotiated by the Developers with the PO 'without affecting the Sprint Goal'. The one-person rule and persuasion clause (L80) concern the Product Backlog.
findings.fix: correct: The engineering manager's mid-Sprint reordering overrides the Developers' plan (the Sprint Backlog is "a plan by and for the Developers" [V]) and bypasses the Product Owner, the single owner of the Product Backlog ("The Product Owner is one person, not a committee" [V]). Managers influence the Product Owner by persuasion; they do not edit the Sprint Backlog or Sprint scope directly.

findings.claim: Transparency check (Key Concept 2). The burn-down chart has been the team's primary decision tool.
findings.failure_mode: mis-cited to the wrong Key Concept
findings.evidence: The burn-down-as-input point is Key Concept 12 (forecasting does not replace empiricism; deep ref L113), not Key Concept 2 (the three pillars).
findings.fix: correct: Forecasting as input (Key Concept 12).

findings.claim: This is the framework's structural contribution: commitments at the right level make decision-making cheaper at every level below them.
findings.failure_mode: distillation's generalisation attributed to the framework
findings.evidence: Deep ref L171, L198: commitments 'enhance transparency and focus against which progress can be measured'; the Sprint Goal 'creates coherence and focus'. The Guide makes no claim about decision cost across levels.
findings.fix: correct: In this example the Sprint Goal does the work the Guide gives it: it "creates coherence and focus" [V], so requests can be tested against one committed objective.

findings.claim: Overriding Developers' authority over their own sizing and Daily Scrum structure. "No one else tells them how." [V]
findings.failure_mode: truncated quote attached to the wrong concepts
findings.evidence: Deep ref L129: the full sentence is 'No one else tells them how to turn Product Backlog items into Increments of value' (Sprint Planning, Topic Three). Sizing is L181; Daily Scrum structure is L141.
findings.fix: correct: Overriding Developers' authority over how they build, their sizing, and their Daily Scrum structure. "No one else tells them how to turn Product Backlog items into Increments of value." [V]

findings.claim: Jones reads Agile and Scrum critically: the post-1980 evidence collapse means most software-engineering claims, including some about Agile, are folklore-laden.
findings.failure_mode: other source's position overstated
findings.evidence: jones-evidence-based-sweng-deep.md L149: Jones says 'The rarity of measurement data for any of the agile processes means this evidence-based book has little to say about them' [V] (Ch 5.4.3). Scrum does not appear in the Jones deep ref; the folklore examples (L15, L39-41) are the 28-to-1 claim and Halstead/McCabe metrics, not Agile.
findings.fix: correct: Jones sets Agile aside for lack of data: 'The rarity of measurement data for any of the agile processes means this evidence-based book has little to say about them' [V]. Scrum is not discussed.

findings.claim: OpenStax, Organizational Behavior (Ch 13, Ch 14): programmed vs non-programmed decisions, six-step process, groupthink, escalation of commitment
findings.failure_mode: wrong chapters
findings.evidence: openstax-organizational-behavior-deep.md L177-L204: these are all Ch 6 (6.3, 6.4, 6.6). Ch 13 is power and politics; Ch 14 is conflict and negotiation (L428, L430).
findings.fix: correct: OpenStax, Organizational Behavior (Ch 6)

findings.section: Integration with Other References, Business Ethics
findings.claim: Mitchell-Agle-Wood salience (power, legitimacy, urgency) is the theory Scrum's single-owner constraint operationalises
findings.failure_mode: concept attributed to the wrong corpus source
findings.evidence: openstax-business-ethics-deep.md L124-126 (Ch 3.3) gives a power x interest matrix plus exigency; Mitchell-Agle-Wood does not appear in that deep ref or its converted source. Mitchell-Agle-Wood salience appears only in jones-evidence-based-sweng-deep.md L153 (Ch 5.4.5), without the power/legitimacy/urgency triad.
findings.fix: correct: Business Ethics' stakeholder prioritisation (a power x interest matrix, with exigency raising priority; Ch 3.3) is the theory the Product Owner applies when ordering many stakeholders' needs in one Product Backlog.

findings.section: What this reference does not cover
findings.claim: cross-team scaling (no SAFe, LeSS, Nexus, or Scrum of Scrums detail; the Guide stops at the team level)
findings.failure_mode: source scope misstated
findings.evidence: Deep ref L62: teams that grow too large 'should consider reorganizing into multiple cohesive Scrum Teams, each focused on the same product ... share the same Product Goal, Product Backlog, and Product Owner'. L219: 'If there are multiple Scrum Teams working together on a product, they must mutually define and comply with the same Definition of Done'. This distillation itself quotes the second at L97.
findings.fix: correct: cross-team scaling (no SAFe, LeSS, Nexus or Scrum of Scrums detail; the Guide says only that multiple Scrum Teams on one product share one Product Goal, Product Backlog, Product Owner and Definition of Done)

findings.claim: The Guide is intentionally minimal: 13 pages in the 2020 edition.
findings.failure_mode: count does not match deep ref
findings.evidence: Deep ref L7, L9, L265: 'Single 14-page guide'; 'all 14 pages'.
findings.fix: correct: 14 pages in the 2020 edition.

findings.claim: the Guide is explicit that "non-empirical decisions" (routine, well-understood problems) do not need a Sprint container.
findings.failure_mode: fabricated quotation and position attributed to the source
findings.evidence: 'non-empirical' does not occur in the converted source or the deep ref. The Guide says nothing about when Scrum is not needed; it says only that Scrum is for complex problems (deep L25).
findings.fix: correct: The framework is designed for complex problems; the Guide does not say what to use for routine, well-understood work.

notes: Every other [V] quotation checked word for word against sources/converted/scrum-guide-2020.md; all exact (including the capitalised substring 'Implementing only parts of Scrum is possible, the result is not Scrum' at L110/L159, which is a contiguous substring after 'While'). Integration rows checked: Letaw (Ch 1.2.2 cites the Guide; methods in Ch 2-3) holds; PoM Deming/Shewhart PDCA (Ch 17.2) holds; Entrepreneurship lean startup build-measure-learn (Ch 10.1) holds; Jones, OB and Business Ethics rows drift (D021-D023). Recurring pattern: 'can lead to' hardened to 'produce/will/yields' three times (D002, D007, D011). Two phrases in quotation marks are not in the source (D014, D026).
